== Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:12-237

\section{Literals}
\seclabel{literals}

\note{We need to check whether the various types and values defined in this section are still correct.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{LiteralExpr} &::=& \texttt{(} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{NumericLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{CharLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{StringLiteralExpr}\\
\end{Grammar}

Fortress provides boolean literals, \TYP{()} literal, character literals,
string literals, and numeric literals.  Literals are values; they do not
require evaluation.

\note{From here, copied from F1.0$\beta$.}

The literal \VAR{false} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{false}\rrbracket}.
The literal \VAR{true} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
\note{And these are the only values of those types.}

The literal \EXP{()} is the only value with type \TYP{()}.
Whether any given occurrence of \TYP{()} refers to the value \EXP{()} or
to the type \TYP{()} is determined by context.

A character literal has type \TYP{Character}.
Each character literal consists of an abstract character in
\unicode~\cite{Unicode},
enclosed in single quotation marks (for example, `\txt{a}', `\txt{A}',
`\txt{\$}', `\txt{$\alpha$}', `\txt{$\oplus$}').
\marginnote{This is not true: Character literals include ``\b'' and
``LATIN CAPITAL A'', which do not ``consist of'' an abstract character enclosed in
single quotation marks.  I think it's better to remove most of this discussion and
direct the reader to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.
This section should be about {\bf semantics} of literals:
their values and types.}
The single quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' single quotation marks
or a pair of ordinary apostrophe characters (for example, \txt{'a'}, \txt{'A'}, \txt{'\$'}, \txt{'$\alpha$'}, \txt{'$\oplus$'}).
See \secref{preprocessing-character-literals} for a description of how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within character literals,
for example `\txt{APOSTROPHE}' and `\txt{GREEK\_CAPITAL\_LETTER\_GAMMA}'.

A string literal has type \TYP{String}.
Each string literal is a sequence of \unicode\ characters enclosed in double
quotation marks (for example,
``\txt{Hello, world!}'' or ``\txt{$\pi\thinspace r^2$}'').
\marginnote{Again, I think this paragraph should mostly be eliminated and replaced with a pointer to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.

Here's a sentence I wrote as a replacement:
``A string literal (i.e., a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks---see Section 5.10 for details) has type String.''}
The double quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' double  quotation marks
or a pair of ``neutral'' double-quote characters (for example,
\txt{"Hello, world!"} or \txt{"$\pi\thinspace r^2$"}).
\secref{preprocessing-string-literals} also describes how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within string literals.
One may also use the escape sequences \txt{{\char'134}b} and \txt{{\char'134}t}
and \txt{{\char'134}n} and \txt{{\char'134}f} and \txt{{\char'134}r} as described in \cite{JLS}.


\note{We may want to eliminate the distinction between simple and compound numerals,
and just distinguish them by whether they have a radix point or not, when necessary
(i.e., ``Numerals may have a radix point.'').  Again,
that distinction is primarily a syntactic one, and can be discussed there if appropriate.}
Numeric literals in Fortress are referred to as \emph{numerals},
corresponding to various expressible numbers.
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}


A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.

The type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ relaxes the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ and
includes two extra values, \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0} (sometimes called ``the
infinite rational'' and ``the indefinite rational'').
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
If a value of type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is assigned to a
variable of type $\mathbb{Q}$, a \TYP{DivisionByZero} is thrown
at run time if the value is \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0}.
The type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} includes all of \EXP{1/0}, \EXP{-1/0}, and
\EXP{0/0}.
The advantage of $\mathbb{Q}^{\#}$ is that it is closed under the rational
operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#} are written as \txt{QQ}, \txt{QQ\_star}, and
\txt{QQ\_splat}, respectively.
See \secref{advanced-rationals} for definitions of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*},
and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#}.



\subsection{Pi}
\seclabel{pi}

The object named \EXP{\pi} (or \txt{pi}) may be used to represent the ratio
of the circumference of a circle to its diameter rather than a specific
floating-point value or interval value.
In Fortress, \EXP{\pi} has type
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}.
When used in a floating-point computation, it becomes
a floating-point value of the appropriate precision; when used in an interval
computation, it becomes an interval of the appropriate precision.

\subsection{Infinity and Zero}

The object named \EXP{\infty} has type \EXP{\TYP{ExtendedIntegerValue}\llbracket\VAR{true},0,\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
One can negate \EXP{\infty} to get a negative infinity.

\note{What about spaces?  That is, is ``- 0'' treated the same as ``-0'', for example?}
Negating the literal \EXP{0} produces a special negative-zero object,
which refuses to participate in static arithmetic
(discussed in \secref{static-expr}).  It
has type \TYP{NegativeZero}.  The main thing it is good for is coercion to
a floating-point number (discussed in
\chapref{conversions-coercions}).
(Negating any other zero-valued expression simply produces zero.)

== Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:12-255

\section{Literals}
\seclabel{literals}

\note{We need to check whether the various types and values defined in this section are still correct.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{LiteralExpr} &::=& \texttt{(} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{NumericLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{CharLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{StringLiteralExpr}\\
\end{Grammar}

Fortress provides boolean literals, \TYP{()} literal, character literals,
string literals, and numeric literals.  Literals are values; they do not
require evaluation.

\note{From here, copied from F1.0$\beta$.}

The literal \VAR{false} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{false}\rrbracket}.
The literal \VAR{true} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
\note{And these are the only values of those types.}

The literal \EXP{()} is the only value with type \TYP{()}.
Whether any given occurrence of \TYP{()} refers to the value \EXP{()} or
to the type \TYP{()} is determined by context.

A character literal has type \TYP{Character}.
Each character literal consists of an abstract character in
\unicode~\cite{Unicode},
enclosed in single quotation marks (for example, `\txt{a}', `\txt{A}',
`\txt{\$}', `\txt{$\alpha$}', `\txt{$\oplus$}').
\marginnote{This is not true: Character literals include ``\b'' and
``LATIN CAPITAL A'', which do not ``consist of'' an abstract character enclosed in
single quotation marks.  I think it's better to remove most of this discussion and
direct the reader to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.
This section should be about {\bf semantics} of literals:
their values and types.}
The single quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' single quotation marks
or a pair of ordinary apostrophe characters (for example, \txt{'a'}, \txt{'A'}, \txt{'\$'}, \txt{'$\alpha$'}, \txt{'$\oplus$'}).
See \secref{preprocessing-character-literals} for a description of how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within character literals,
for example `\txt{APOSTROPHE}' and `\txt{GREEK\_CAPITAL\_LETTER\_GAMMA}'.

A string literal has type \TYP{String}.
Each string literal is a sequence of \unicode\ characters enclosed in double
quotation marks (for example,
``\txt{Hello, world!}'' or ``\txt{$\pi\thinspace r^2$}'').
\marginnote{Again, I think this paragraph should mostly be eliminated and replaced with a pointer to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.

Here's a sentence I wrote as a replacement:
``A string literal (i.e., a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks---see Section 5.10 for details) has type String.''}
The double quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' double  quotation marks
or a pair of ``neutral'' double-quote characters (for example,
\txt{"Hello, world!"} or \txt{"$\pi\thinspace r^2$"}).
\secref{preprocessing-string-literals} also describes how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within string literals.
One may also use the escape sequences \txt{{\char'134}b} and \txt{{\char'134}t}
and \txt{{\char'134}n} and \txt{{\char'134}f} and \txt{{\char'134}r} as described in \cite{JLS}.


\note{We may want to eliminate the distinction between simple and compound numerals,
and just distinguish them by whether they have a radix point or not, when necessary
(i.e., ``Numerals may have a radix point.'').  Again,
that distinction is primarily a syntactic one, and can be discussed there if appropriate.}
Numeric literals in Fortress are referred to as \emph{numerals},
corresponding to various expressible numbers.
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
coercion from it.
\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
that \library\ give a numeral.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.}

\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}


A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.
Relaxing the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ adds three more values, which
$\mathbb{Q}$ also includes: \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0}, the infinite rationals,
and \EXP{0/0}, the indefinite rational.
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
The advantage of these values is that $\mathbb{Q}$ is closed under the rational
operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is written as \txt{QQ}.
See \secref{basic-rationals} for its operations.
\revision{revival-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} as three types,
said that a value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} assigned to a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero} at run time if it is \EXP{1/0}
or \EXP{-1/0}, gave the ASCII names \txt{QQ\_star} and \txt{QQ\_splat}, and
pointed to \secref{advanced-rationals} for the definitions.
The three are one type now, as in \library\ (\secref{basic-rationals}), so no
such assignment converts or throws; that is also the answer to the margin
note's question whether \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} are related by
subtyping or by coercion.}



\subsection{Pi}
\seclabel{pi}

The object named \EXP{\pi} (or \txt{pi}) may be used to represent the ratio
of the circumference of a circle to its diameter rather than a specific
floating-point value or interval value.
In Fortress, \EXP{\pi} has type
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}.
When used in a floating-point computation, it becomes
a floating-point value of the appropriate precision; when used in an interval
computation, it becomes an interval of the appropriate precision.

\subsection{Infinity and Zero}

The object named \EXP{\infty} has type \EXP{\TYP{ExtendedIntegerValue}\llbracket\VAR{true},0,\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
One can negate \EXP{\infty} to get a negative infinity.

\note{What about spaces?  That is, is ``- 0'' treated the same as ``-0'', for example?}
Negating the literal \EXP{0} produces a special negative-zero object,
which refuses to participate in static arithmetic
(discussed in \secref{static-expr}).  It
has type \TYP{NegativeZero}.  The main thing it is good for is coercion to
a floating-point number (discussed in
\chapref{conversions-coercions}).
(Negating any other zero-valued expression simply produces zero.)

== Specification/basic/expressions/constant.tex:39-93

\subsection{Types of Static Expressions}

There are three groups of traits that describe literals
and static expressions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{literal} traits, which describe boolean,
  character, string, and numerals.  For example, the literal \VAR{true} has
  trait \EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket} and a
  character literal has trait \TYP{Character}.
See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals.

\item The \emph{constant} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals and operators (described in
\secref{constant-values});
the type of a constant expression encodes the value of the expression.
For example, the type of a constant expression \EXP{3+5},
%IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]
\EXP{\TYP{IntegerConstant}\llbracket\VAR{false}, 3+5\rrbracket},
encodes the value of the expression; the operator \EXP{+} is
used in the static arguments.  When an operator is not supported in static
arguments, \library\ can still encode the value of the expression by
providing a specific constant trait such as
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}
(described in \secref{pi}).



\item The \emph{static} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals, operators (described in
\secref{constant-values}), and \KWD{bool}, \KWD{nat},
and \KWD{int} parameters; here the type
does not encode the value of the expression, but the value of the
expression can nevertheless be known statically if specific
values are specified for the static parameters.  Also, in situations
where the type of an expression composed solely from literals and
operators nevertheless cannot be described by a constant trait, then a
static trait may be used to describe it instead.
For example, a static expression \EXP{2(3+m)} where \VAR{m} is a
\KWD{nat} parameter has trait \TYP{NaturalStatic}.
\end{enumerate}


The only operation on literals that produces a new literal (as opposed
to a constant) is concatenation by using the operator \EXP{\|}.
One may concatenate mixed string and
character literals, producing a string literal.
For example, ``\txt{foo}''\EXP{\|}''\txt{bar}'' yields ``\txt{foobar}''.
One may also concatenate two natural numerals
of the same radix, producing a new natural numeral of that radix.
For example, \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16} \| \mathtt{0de}_{16}} yields \EXP{\mathtt{deadc0de}_{16}}.

Every literal trait extends an appropriate constant trait, and every
constant trait extends an appropriate static trait.  So every
literal is also a constant expression, and every constant expression
is a static expression.

== Specification/basic/inference.tex:299-437

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

This chapter does not yet describe:
\begin{itemize}
\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
\item a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter that neither an argument nor the
expected type fixes;
\item the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine
(\secref{reduction-expr}): the rule above gives a static parameter of the big
operator that nothing at the call fixes its bounds, not the type of the
elements;
\item whether an argument whose declared parameter type mentions a static
parameter inside another type may be converted where only a conversion of its
elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such
an argument fixes the parameter by subtyping and is not converted;
\item an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
the body of a \KWD{for} loop;
\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}).
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 29~September 2026
named here also an expression that a local declaration precedes in a block, an
\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase} expression
and a call written by loose juxtaposition, its text of 8~October 2026 also
the body of a \KWD{label} expression, and its text of 9~October 2026 also an
argument of another call, to which the list of contexts in
\secref{static-arg-inference} now gives an expected type where the argument is
itself a call with inferred static arguments and the enclosing call
is not accepted without it.}
\revision{revival-inference}{The compiled type checker instantiates a type
parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes at the
intersection of its upper bounds, as \secref{static-arg-inference} says; on the
compiled path, as in the interpreter, a type parameter declared without an
\KWD{extends} clause is bounded by \TYP{Any}, so that a call that fixes such a
parameter by the expected type alone may fix it at a type that \TYP{Object}
excludes, such as \TYP{()}.
A reduction's big operator is an argument of the call that the reduction's
desugaring makes, so it has an expected type only as such an argument has one:
the compiled type checker instantiates a generic big operator whose static
argument the reduction does not write at its bound, and at the reduction's
expected type only where the reduction's type at that bound does not fit it,
and it refuses the reduction where the big operator has no instance at its
bound, as one whose bound mentions its own static parameter has none (row~425
of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter instantiates a type parameter of a function that nothing at a
call fixes at its bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and one whose bound mentions
other static parameters at that bound with their instances, with two
exceptions: a type parameter that only the bound of a type parameter that the
arguments fix mentions, as \EXP{A \KWD{extends} T} mentions \VAR{T}, it
instantiates at the arguments' type, not at its bound, since it has no expected
type to fix it (row~592 of the revival's gap ledger); and a type parameter
declared with several bounds that it cannot meet, as two bounds neither of which
is a subtype of the other, it erases to \TYP{BottomType} (row~591).
A type parameter whose bound mentions the type parameter itself, as the big
operators $\sum$ and $\prod$ declare theirs, and that nothing at a call fixes,
it leaves open: it does not instantiate it, and it admits every value where it
checks a value against that type, as an argument, a variable declared with that
type, a \KWD{typecase} clause or a type assertion.
The big operator that a reduction or a comprehension invokes without its
static arguments it instantiates as the desugaring by the type \VAR{N} of the
expression would (\secref{reduction-expr}), with run-time types in place of the
static type that it does not have: by the declared type of the local variable,
or the declared return type of the top-level or local function, whose value the
reduction or the comprehension is, also as the last expression of a block, where
that type fixes the big operator's result type; otherwise by the join of the run-time types of
the elements that its generator clauses give, which it collects before it
reduces them; and where there is no element, at the bound of each static
parameter, or open where the bound mentions the parameter itself.
So an empty sum that is the value of a function declared \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
is the \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} zero, and the library's set reductions
\EXP{\bigcup} and \EXP{\bigcap} run on sets of their elements' type; but an
empty reduction that no declared type directs takes the identity of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the expression, and an empty
comprehension that no declared type directs is built at the bound, a list
comprehension as a \EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket\TYP{Any}\rrbracket} (row~716 of the
revival's gap ledger); a comprehension that no declared type reaches, such as
the value of a top-level variable, a field, a method or a function expression,

argument of a call, is

enclosing expression may not admit (rows~20, 510 and~717).

\TYP{BigReduction}, \TYP{Comprehension} and \TYP{BigOperator} it instantiates
through the one of those three that its declared result extends, with that
trait's static arguments.

\TYP{BottomType}, so that a type parameter that only its result fixes is
instantiated there (row~587); and it instantiates a static parameter of a
generic method that only the expected type would fix, as one of a generic
function, at its bound (row~510), a method that a trait declares among them.

checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}

\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**. Until the **switch-over**, the compiled path uses its own small library, the **prelude**; after it, the interpreter's library, the **one library**.
- A **numeral** is a number written in the program, `3` or `0.5`. A **numeral type** is the type the checker gives it while it types the program: today `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`, after this batch, in the one library, the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` below `Numeral`. The **four numbers** are the Draft's `n`, `m`, `r` and `v`: the digit count, the digits after the radix point, the radix, and the digits read as one integer.
- A place **fixes a type** when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, or is a numeral type; elsewhere the numeral takes its **default**, `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, `RR64` with a radix point (P-173).

- **The count** and **the distance** are the checker's errors on the one library: 0 and 0 at climb batch 28's gate, the distance with no crash (F-53).
- A **rung** is one change, built by one worker and checked by a second agent, the skeptic; the **gather** composes the rungs; a **guard** is a test that passes before the change and after it. **Appendix I** is the specification's appendix of changes.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung of this batch changes a line of it, and by reading no bit (the judgement's appendix).

### The scope: six rungs, the decided design whole

The record proposes six rungs:

- **N**, the numeral types in the one library and walk's numerals: P-174's names and fields, P-76's and P-172's conversions with their pairs, the 24 glue bindings gone (P-169), and P-173's walk half, place by place.
- **C**, the checker's half of P-173 and P-174: the default, the narrowest default for a type parameter, the numeral types unwritable but as a parameter type, the static range refusal, no chain, a size as a `ZZ32`. It lands only with N.
- **F**, the fold, on both paths, with one rounding and the once-per-class coercion on the compiled path.
- **G**, row 364's way A: walk's generics and messages at the trait.
- **S**, P-171: the strings.
- **T**, the specification. It lands only with N, C, F and S.

The reasons, one by one:

1. **The library and walk's numerals go in one rung, N, not two.** PLAN's line puts walk's numerals in a rung of their own that lands with the library's. But every rung branches from the base (PLAN, "The principle for the batches"), and on the base's library a float numeral is an `RR64` (`value object FloatLiteral extends RR64`), `QQ` takes no float numeral and `RR32` none at all, so a walk rung built there could test neither its tie, nor its `QQ` and `RR32` places, nor the numeral objects a program's coercion receives. And the library change alone fails 71 of walk's 791 tests (the prototype, section 4.5). So the two change together, and N holds them, with the two checker edits the library needs: the names switched by library, and the float tie rule, without which the library alone makes two ties (the prototype, step 1a).
2. **The checker's default and refusals go in C, against the prelude.** Its rules are the same on either library, so its compiled tests run on the base's prelude, and its count on the base's library. It lands only with N: the two change one behaviour, a numeral's type, in its two halves, which the batch rule lands together (`references/batch.md`, "The go"); without N, the checker would default and refuse the numeral types against a library that still declares `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic and `FloatLiteral` below `RR64`, a state the design never names.
3. **The pairs stay, C builds no chain, and the prototype's step 5 stays in its narrow form.** With the 15 pairs over the integer numeral and new pairs over the float numeral, the prototype's checker counts 0 and the distance 0, with and without its step 5 and its chained coercion, and every comparison of a number with a numeral reaches its pair but one: `r = 0` for an `RR32`, which declares no coercion from an integer numeral (probe 1). P-76 has `RR32` convert from it; N adds the coercion and its pair. Step 5, a numeral's conversion into its own default ranked as no coercion, stays (fork C4, the Fable review's change): P-173 reads `gg(5, w)` by P-49 as both declarations fitting the numeral as it is, and walk's dispatch keeps that rule (fork N6), so the checker's static choice and the compiled dispatch agree on `ee(5)`.
4. **The fold runs on both paths.** Its phase runs today on the compiled path only. Put in walk's phase order at the base, it passes 789 of walk's 791 tests; the two write `ZZ32` operations on numerals alone and mean `ZZ32` arithmetic (probe 2). On the way, probe 3 found two defects of today's fold, a compile that stops at `3 CHOOSE 5` and a wrapping `BOXPLUS` folded as exact addition, both F's.
5. **G, S and T.** G is one walk rung by the row 364 review, independent of the numerals but for one test key (section 4, "The rule the rungs keep"). S is one small rung with its fold. T describes the merged design, so it lands only with the four rungs whose code it describes.
6. **Six rungs keep the gather in bounds.** Section 4, "The rule the rungs keep", gives each rung's place in each shared file: N and C share `Functionals.scala` only at named functions, N and G share `EvaluatorBase.java` at two places 500 lines apart, N and S share `Evaluator.java` at two methods 600 lines apart, C and F share `CodeGen.java` at methods 2,100 lines and more apart.

### The three points with no default on record

Each is named as a fork with the record's default and its reason (section 3). None holds the launch: each can be undone, none reverses a decision of his.

**Point 1, review-queue item 443: may a value of a numeral type be bound by inference inside a coercion's body, `t = x` in `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`?** Default: **yes; `t` takes the numeral type** (fork C2). The reason: P-174 says a numeral type is *written* only as a parameter type, and a check of written types does not see an inferred one; the binding adds no numeral value, since the parameter already holds it; refusing it would need a second check over inferred types that protects nothing, since `x` itself can still be passed on. The principles that speak agree: the team's later word, the prelude, binds `IntLiteral` anywhere, and the library writes it as a variable's and a return type. Not consequential. The Fable review recommends the default (`climb-batch-29-review.md`, section 1).

**Point 2, review-queue item 447: the constant chapter's concatenation of two natural numerals, `deadc_16 || 0de_16` giving `deadc0de_16` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/constant.tex:80-82`).** Default: **folded, as the Draft says, in rung F** (fork F4): two natural numerals of one radix joined by `||` fold into one natural numeral, whose four numbers are the digits of both. The reason: the Draft's sentence is the one team word on it, beside the string concatenation that P-171 folds; neither implementation contradicts it, they never built it; and the four numbers P-174 keeps hold the digit count, leading zeros included, which the concatenation needs, so nothing of the binary chapter's static width is involved. Its cost is a case of the fold and one test. Not consequential: only the Draft speaks, and it is kept as written. The Fable review recommends the default: at the base `deadc_16 || 0de_16` finds no `||` under walk ("Failed to find any matching overload, args = (912092: ZZ32,222: ZZ32)"), so the fold adds what no path has and changes no program that runs today (`climb-batch-29-review.md`, section 1).

**Point 3: does `RadixPointNumeral` declare `asFloat`? P-165's list names `NaturalNumeral` and not it.** Default: **yes, with one rounding, as `NaturalNumeral` declares it** (fork N4). The reason: P-165's list came from `IntLiteral`'s own `asFloat` when `FloatLiteral` extended `RR64` and inherited `RR64`'s, so the list's silence is history, not a choice; today's `FloatLiteral` declares `asFloat` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:213-214`), so dropping it would change `asFloat(x)` at that type, against P-165's "unchanged at every concrete type"; and the library's pattern gives every number type and the other numeral type the method. **Consequential**, since it reads P-165's list anew; it bends nothing and lands with its default. The record writer would add `RadixPointNumeral` to P-165's list. The Fable review recommends the default (`climb-batch-29-review.md`, section 1).

### The forks he may want to see

Two forks besides point 3 are consequential by the `coordinator` skill's rule (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"). Each lands with its default overnight, by the go rule, and goes on the review list:

- **Fork N1, the numeral types as plain value objects with Fortress fields.** `NaturalNumeral(digits, radix, digitValue)` and `RadixPointNumeral(digits, fractionDigits, radix, digitValue)`, in `FortressLibrary` beside `Ratio`, under `trait Numeral`, with no binding: walk builds one only where a numeral meets a parameter of a numeral type, and the compiled path after the switch-over constructs one as any object, "invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser" in his words. The way not taken: traits, as the prelude declares its two, with walk's native objects and compiled run-time classes below them and the four getters on helpers by P-167's device, P-164's form for a value a Java class holds, the form both team libraries gave their numerals. Consequential because the principles split: the team's two libraries back Java-held numerals, the library's own `Ratio` and P-174's words back fields. The Fable review recommends the default (`climb-batch-29-review.md`, section 1).
- **The deferrals to the switch-over on the compiled path (forks F5, F6, F7).** The compiled path reads the prelude until the switch-over, which declares neither the four numbers nor the pairs nor `QQ`. So three pieces of the decided design reach the compiled path only then, each with a PLAN line: a program's coercion there receives today's compiled numeral value, without its four numbers; the pairs' conversion of a numeral is not folded at a call; and the compiled `SEQV` of two numeral values by their reduced value. Walk builds all three now. Not consequential by the rule, since nothing observable differs before the switch-over; listed because P-173 names the pairs' fold. The decided design is to be written in the revision form, with Appendix I entries that name what it contradicts in the Working Draft and what it changes in form.

**The decisions this rung builds.** P-173, P-174, P-76, P-172, P-171, P-165 and P-40, each in its sentences; P-96, the revision form; P-26, whose bend P-173's entry owns as his weighing. - `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:74-90`, the box `revival-int-float`, and `:98-101`, the default as a rule beside coercion.

57	A string literal has type \TYP{String}.
58	Each string literal is a sequence of \unicode\ characters enclosed in double
59	quotation marks (for example,
60	``\txt{Hello, world!}'' or ``\txt{$\pi\thinspace r^2$}'').
61	\marginnote{Again, I think this paragraph should mostly be eliminated and replaced with a pointer to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.
62	
63	Here's a sentence I wrote as a replacement:
64	``A string literal (i.e., a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks---see Section 5.10 for details) has type String.''}
65	The double quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' double  quotation marks
66	or a pair of ``neutral'' double-quote characters (for example,
67	\txt{"Hello, world!"} or \txt{"$\pi\thinspace r^2$"}).
68	\secref{preprocessing-string-literals} also describes how names of
69	characters may be used rather than actual characters within string literals.
70	One may also use the escape sequences \txt{{\char'134}b} and \txt{{\char'134}t}
71	and \txt{{\char'134}n} and \txt{{\char'134}f} and \txt{{\char'134}r} as described in \cite{JLS}.
72	

78	Numeric literals in Fortress are referred to as \emph{numerals},
79	corresponding to various expressible numbers.
80	Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
81	(as described in \secref{numerals}).
82	
83	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
84	has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
85	interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
86	the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
87	\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
88	have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?
89	
90	What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
91	and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?
92	
93	We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
94	All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
95	And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
96	}
97	
98	\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
99	Or is that just part of lexical structure?
100	(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
101	type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
102	for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}
103	
104	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
105	digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
106	radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
107	where $v$ is
108	the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.
109	
110	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
111	of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
112	the radix point) has type
113	\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
114	the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
115	interpreted in radix ten.
116	
117	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
118	of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
119	the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
120	be the radix) has the following type:
121	\begin{Fortress}
122	\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
123	\end{Fortress}
124	where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
125	deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.
126	
127	Every numeral also has type
128	\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
129	for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.
130	
131	
132	Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
133	because, as in common mathematical usage,
134	we expect them to be polymorphic.
135	For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
136	converting it immediately to a floating-point number
137	may lose precision.
138	If that numeral is used in an expression
139	involving floating-point intervals,
140	it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
141	Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
142	This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
143	interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
144	(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
145	in Fortress).
146	\Library\ define coercions
147	from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
148	and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
149	In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
150	\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
151	(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
152	(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
153	coercion from it.
154	\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
155	the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
156	that \library\ give a numeral.
157	The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
158	\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
159	path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
160	The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
161	The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
162	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
163	does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
164	\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
165	checker.}
166	
167	
168	\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
169	In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
170	a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
171	this is true regardless of whether
172	the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
173	$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
174	whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
175	are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
176	Fortress.
177	
178	\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
179	Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
180	literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
181	The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
182	(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
183	Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
184	$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
185	such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
186	is a static expression whose value is rational.
187	If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
188	computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
189	converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
190	at most one floating-point rounding error.
191	But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
192	not just at compile time.
193	\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
194	I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
195	In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
196	performed exactly at run time?}
197	
198	
199	A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
200	that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';

# Rung V: the integer conversions (rung-integer-conversions)

- problem: rows 858 and 859, a low-bits name missing on a type and reached by coercion, and row 502, ZZ's widen keeping the low 64 bits (`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:572`, `:573`, `:557`), measured in `explorations/reviews/integer-conversions-2026-11-06.md:281-332`
- spec: `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-45` at 157323e51 (the explicit conversions, narrow's sentence), beside "For integer results, overflow throws an IntegerOverflow." (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:155`)
- precedent: QQ's `ceiling` and `truncate`, a test and `throw DivisionByZero` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:635`, `:640`); the prelude's `getter asZZ32(): ZZ32 = jLongOverflowingToInt(self)` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:581`); powerCount32's sign test of `signed(c)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:747-751`); the prelude's `trait IntLiteral` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:883-889`)
- deviation: ZZ's asZZ64 and asNN64 bind two new helpers, `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToLong` and `bigOverflowingToUnsignedLong`, beyond fork V1's three pairs, since after the deletion ZZ has no low-bits form for a Fortress body to wrap (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java:147-157`)
- deviation: `Library/QuickCheck.fss:322` on `.asZZ64` raises IntegerOverflow for a ZZ outside ZZ64, where `widen` kept the low 64 bits; under walk no generator makes one (row 387) (`Library/QuickCheck.fss:322`)
- deviation: two calls of ZZ's narrow outside the named declarations moved, in countNN32 and exponentNN32 (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:400`, `:419`)
- deviation: the getters stand before each type's methods, which the parser requires: 'Field/getter/setter declarations should come before method declarations.' (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:500`, `:568`, `:644`, `:719`; `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:135`)
- historical: `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `Library/Format.fss`, `Library/QuickCheck.fss`, `ProjectFortress/demos/sudoku.fss`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java`, `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1`)

Commits on `wip/rung-integer-conversions`: 2d49a587 (the code and its tests), 227979aa (the specification). The worktree was seeded by `seed-worktree.sh` (exit 0, 4 s).

## What changed and why

P-161, option 6, whole, and P-169's eight numeral bindings.

**The 25 getters**, each declared in the api at the component's header, each a getter before the type's methods:

| type | asZZ32 | asZZ64 | asNN32 | asNN64 | asZZ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ZZ32 (`FortressLibrary.fss:771-775`, `.fsi:568-572`) | `= self` | `widen(self)` | Fortress, raises below 0 | Fortress, raises below 0 | `big(self)` |
| ZZ64 (`.fss:877-883`, `.fsi:644-648`) | helper `simpleIntArith.longOverflowingToInt` | `= self` | helper `simpleUnsignedIntArith.longOverflowingToUnsignedInt` | Fortress, raises below 0 | `big(self)` |
| NN32 (`FortressBuiltin.fss:430-437`, `.fsi:135-139`) | Fortress, raises at 2^31 and up | `signed(widen(self))` | `= self` | `widen(self)` | `big(self)` |
| NN64 (`.fss:983-994`, `.fsi:500-504`) | Fortress, raises at 2^31 and up | Fortress, raises at 2^63 and up | helper `simpleUnsignedIntArith.longOverflowingToUnsignedInt` | `= self` | `big(self)` |
| ZZ (`.fss:1096-1102`, `.fsi:719-723`) | `self.asZZ64.asZZ32` | helper `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToLong` (new) | `self.asNN64.asNN32` | helper `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.bigOverflowingToUnsignedLong` (new) | `= self` |

So 5 identities, 7 equal to the coercions (each the coercion's own one-call body), and 13 that can raise: 6 Fortress bodies, a sign or range test and `throw IntegerOverflow` around the low-bits form, as QQ's `truncate` throws `DivisionByZero`; 3 on the existing checked helpers of fork V1; 2 on new helpers; 2 compositions over them. The Java signatures: `public static int longOverflowingToInt(long l)` (`simpleIntArith.java:106`), `public static int longOverflowingToUnsignedInt(long l)` (`simpleUnsignedIntArith.java:87`), and the new `public static long bigOverflowingToLong(BigInteger a)` and `public static long bigOverflowingToUnsignedLong(BigInteger a)` (`simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java:148`, `:154`), which raise `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntegerOverflow` as the other helpers do. Walk carries ZZ in BigInteger, ZZ64 and NN64 in long, NN32 in int; the compiled rewrite passes an NN32 or NN64 result through its transfer helper.

**The four bitsAs getters**: bitsAsNN32 of ZZ32 and bitsAsNN64 of ZZ64 are `unsigned(self)`, bitsAsZZ32 of NN32 and bitsAsZZ64 of NN64 `signed(self)` (`FortressLibrary.fss:776`, `:884`, `:995`; `FortressBuiltin.fss:438`).

**The low-bits names, newly declared** (fork V5, option 1's nine): narrow and unsigned of NN32 `= self`, big of NN32 `big(signed(widen(self)))` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:523-525`, `.fsi:191-193`); widen and unsigned of NN64 `= self`, big of NN64 `do z: ZZ = self; z end` (`FortressLibrary.fss:1075-1077`, `.fsi:555-557`); signed of ZZ32 and of ZZ64 `= self` (`.fss:862`, `:973`; `.fsi:631`, `:706`); big of ZZ `= self` (`.fss:1189`, `.fsi:772`). ZZ has neither narrow nor widen.

**Deleted**: ZZ's narrow and widen, on the glue `BigNum$ToZZ32` and `BigNum$ToZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1150-1154` and `.fsi:744-745` at 157323e51).

**ZZ32's big** names `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.makeZZfromZZ32` (`FortressLibrary.fss:860-861`), not the glue `Long$ToBigNum`.

**IntLiteral's 8** (`FortressBuiltin.fss:544-551`, `:557`, `:570-574`), with their api lines unchanged:

    getter asZZ32(): ZZ32 = self.asZZ.asZZ32

50	\secref{resolving-coercion}) is well-defined.  Fortress provides
51	implicit coercions for tuple types and arrow types (described in
52	\secref{coercion-tuple-arrow}).  Fortress also provides an additional
53	feature of coercion that allows ``widest-need'' evaluation of
54	numerical expressions (described in \secref{widening}).
55	
56	\section{Principles of Coercion}
57	\seclabel{coercion}
58	
59	In certain situations it is convenient to be able to use a value of
60	one type \VAR{T} as if it were a value of another type \VAR{U} even
61	though \VAR{T} is not a subtype of \VAR{U}.  For example, it is
62	convenient to be able to use an integer-valued expression
63	in a floating-point expression even though its
64	type is not a subtype of any floating-point type.  Fortress supports
65	the automatic conversion of values of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and of integer
66	numerals, to the floating-point type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (the technical term for this kind of automatic
67	conversion is coercion); a value of any other integer type is converted to
68	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} explicitly (\secref{basic-rationals}).  In
69	this way one can write \EXP{(x + 1)/2} rather than \EXP{(x +
70	1.0)/2.0}, for example.  Such coercion applies generally to function
71	and method (collectively called as functional) calls as well as to
72	operators; one can write \EXP{\ln 2} rather than \EXP{\ln 2.0}, or
73	\EXP{\arctan(1,1)} rather than \EXP{\arctan(1.0,1.0)}, for example.
74	\revision{revival-int-float}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
75	Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point
76	values.
77	The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a conversion between number
78	types is a coercion where it is exact and stays explicit where it can lose
79	precision, and \library\ declare the coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from
80	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the decision names the integer numerals too.
81	The conversion from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though exact, stays explicit, since
82	that decision names only \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and the numerals.
83	The examples of this paragraph convert numerals and are unchanged.
84	\Library\ give an integer numeral the type \TYP{IntLiteral}, from which
85	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} coerces, and the compiled type checker types a numeral so
86	(\secref{literals}, \secref{revival-numeral-type}).
87	The interpreter does not yet: it gives an integer numeral outside the range of
88	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} a wider integer type, and so does not yet convert it.
89	The compiled path's own library declares no coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
90	from an integer type or an integer numeral; there \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and integer
91	numerals convert to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} only explicitly, and the other integer types not at all.}
92	
93	One way to think about coercion is that if type \VAR{T} can be coerced
94	to type \VAR{U}, then a value of type \VAR{T} can be used to ``stand
95	in'' for a value of type \VAR{U} in a functional call, for example.  This is
96	different from actually \emph{being} of type \VAR{U}; it means only
97	that, given any value of type \VAR{T}, an appropriate value of type
98	\VAR{U} can be computed to substitute for it.  Also, coercion occurs
99	only when the declared type of the corresponding parameter in the
100	functional declaration is exactly the type \VAR{U} being coerced to
101	 not if it is a supertype of \VAR{U}.  Note, however, that if type
102	 \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{U} then any subtype of \VAR{T}
103	 can also be coerced to type \VAR{U}.
104	
105	Coercion from \VAR{T} to \VAR{U} may occur in an expression context
106	where the context expects the expression to have type \VAR{U} and
107	the type of the expression is a subtype of \VAR{T} except for the following
108	cases:
109	\begin{itemize}
110	\item type ascriptions (see \secref{type-ascription})
111	\item type assumptions (see \secref{type-assumption})
112	\end{itemize}

45	\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
46	\seclabel{static-arg-inference}
47	
48	The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
49	steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
50	instantiated second.
51	
52	\emph{Choice.}
53	The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
54	A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
55	coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
56	applicable to the call.
57	Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
58	with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
59	its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
60	So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
61	declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.
62	
63	\emph{Instantiation.}
64	The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
65	the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
66	\begin{itemize}
67	\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
68	declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
69	\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
70	the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
71	type of the instance.
72	\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
73	declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
74	expected type as well.
75	\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
76	parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
77	takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
78	which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
79	(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
80	substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
96	2019 instantiates a type parameter, which gives the bound.}
97	\item A type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes as
98	above, such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole
99	type, likewise takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound,
100	\TYP{Any} if it has none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type
101	(below), where the call has one, requires of the declared return type.
102	Inference never instantiates a static parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, which
103	programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}).
104	So, for the declaration
105	\EXP{\VAR{stop}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(s\COLON\TYP{String})\COLON{}T}, the
106	variable declaration
107	\EXP{x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = \VAR{stop}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{no}''})} instantiates
108	\VAR{stop} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the same call with no expected type
109	instantiates it at \TYP{Any}.
110	\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 did not
111	describe such a type parameter and left open whether inference may give it
112	\TYP{BottomType}, which the team's draft note at the end of this chapter asks.
113	The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that the rule by which the dispatcher of
114	the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments
115	do not fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, which never instantiates a
116	type parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, is the rule of static inference as well.}
117	\item Every argument is then admitted against the corresponding parameter type
118	of the instance by substitutability: an argument whose type is a subtype of it
119	is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it
120	(\secref{coercion}), as an argument is coerced to the declared type of a
121	parameter of a declaration without static parameters.
122	\end{itemize}
123	The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
124	as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.
125	
126	\emph{The expected type.}
127	A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
128	variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
129	right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
130	type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;

132	local declarations precede it in the block, the block's expected type; as a
133	branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
134	expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression; as a clause of an
135	\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, \TYP{()}, the type that
136	every such clause must have (\secref{if-expr}); as a clause of a
137	\KWD{typecase} expression that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause

11	
12	\section{Static Expressions}
13	\seclabel{static-expr}
14	
15	\note{Of the static expressions in a size, the interpreter computes a sum, a
16	difference, a product and a power exactly, and refuses a power at a negative
17	exponent; the compiled type checker computes each operation on numerals,
18	refusing as out of range a power it does not compute, and compares other size
19	expressions by their written form (\chapref{types}); the compiled path
20	computes a size when it names a class. The compiled type checker does not
21	infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit} static argument.}
22	
23	\emph{Static expressions} denote \emph{static values}.  Conceptually,
24	a static expression is not evaluated while a program is running, and
25	thus its evaluation
26	cannot complete abruptly.  Given instantiations of all static
27	parameters (described in \chapref{trait-parameters}) in scope of a
28	static expression, the value of the static expression can be
29	determined statically.  Static expressions which use a restricted subset of operations can occur as
30	\emph{static arguments} which instantiate static parameters and
31	\KWD{where}-clause constraints (described in \secref{where-clauses}).
32	We define the set of static
33	expressions by first defining the types of static expressions, and
34	distinguishing static values from the closely related literal values.
35	We then describe the expressions that evaluate to the various kinds of
36	static values.
37	
38	
39	\subsection{Types of Static Expressions}
40	
78	\end{enumerate}
79	
80	
81	The only operation on literals that produces a new literal (as opposed
82	to a constant) is concatenation by using the operator \EXP{\|}.
83	One may concatenate mixed string and
84	character literals, producing a string literal.
85	For example, ``\txt{foo}''\EXP{\|}''\txt{bar}'' yields ``\txt{foobar}''.
86	One may also concatenate two natural numerals
87	of the same radix, producing a new natural numeral of that radix.
88	For example, \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16} \| \mathtt{0de}_{16}} yields \EXP{\mathtt{deadc0de}_{16}}.
89	
90	Every literal trait extends an appropriate constant trait, and every
91	constant trait extends an appropriate static trait.  So every
92	literal is also a constant expression, and every constant expression
93	is a static expression.
94	
95	
96	
97	
98	\subsection{Static Expressions and Values}
99	\seclabel{constant-values}
100	
101	Static parameters are static expressions.
102	A \KWD{nat} parameter denotes a value that has type \TYP{NaturalStatic}
103	(which extends \TYP{IntegerStatic}).
104	An \KWD{int} parameter denotes a value that has type \TYP{IntegerStatic}.
105	A \KWD{bool} parameter denotes a value that has type \TYP{BooleanStatic}.
106	
107	
108	Boolean static expressions may be combined using the operators
109	\EXP{\wedge}, \EXP{\vee}, \EXP{\oplus},
110	\EXP{\equiv}, \EXP{\leftrightarrow}, \OPR{NAND}, \OPR{NOR}, \EXP{=},
111	\EXP{\neq}, and \EXP{\rightarrow} (See \appref{operator-precedence} for a
112	discussion of Fortress operators.)
113	to produce other static expressions denoting boolean static expressions.
114	If both operands are boolean constant expressions, then the result is also
115	a boolean constant expression.
116	
117	Character static expressions may be compared using the operators \EXP{<},
118	\EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, \EXP{>},
119	\EXP{=}, and \EXP{\neq} to produce boolean static expressions.  If both
120	operands are character constant expressions, then the result is a boolean
121	constant expression.
122	
123	Numeric static expressions may be compared using the operators \EXP{<},
124	\EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, \EXP{>},
125	\EXP{=}, and \EXP{\neq} to produce boolean static expressions.  If both
126	operands are numeric constant expressions, then the result is a boolean
127	constant expression.
128	
129	Numeric static expressions may be combined using the operators and
130	functions \EXP{+},
131	\EXP{-}, \EXP{\times}, \EXP{\cdot}, \EXP{/}, \EXP{!}, \OPR{MIN}, \OPR{MAX},
132	\EXP{\surd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling},
133	\VAR{hyperfloor}, \VAR{hyperceiling}, \EXP{\gcd}, \TYP{lcm}, \EXP{\sin},
134	\EXP{\cos}, \EXP{\tan}, \EXP{\arcsin}, \EXP{\arccos}, and \EXP{\arctan}
135	to produce new numeric static expressions.  If the result is indeed
136	a numeric static expression, and both operands are numeric constant
137	expressions, then the result is also a numeric constant expression
138	as long as the constant traits provided by \library\ can encode the value
139	of the expression.

19	\emph{Objects} are values that have \objecttypes\ described in
20	\secref{object-traits}.
21	Objects contain \emph{methods} (described in \secref{methods}) and
22	\emph{fields} (described in \secref{fields}).
23	
24	An object is a \emph{value object}, a \emph{reference object},
25	or a \emph{function object}:
26	It is a function object if it has an arrow type,
27	a reference object if it has an object trait type
28	that is not declared with the \KWD{value} modifier
29	(see \secref{value-objects}),
30	and a value object otherwise
31	(i.e., if it has a tuple type, the type (),
32	or an object trait type declared
33	with the \KWD{value} modifier).
34	
35	A value object cannot have mutable fields,
36	and it is completely determined by its type,
37	environment and its fields:
38	Value objects with the same type, environment and fields
39	are indistinguishable.
40	Thus, an implementation may freely copy value objects.
41	Most objects with simple standard types,
42	such as booleans,
43	numeric literals,
44	IEEE floating-point numbers,
45	integers of every precision,
46	and rational numbers are value objects.
47	%
48	In contrast,
49	reference objects are thought to ``reside in memory'',
50	and are identified by an \emph{object reference}.
51	A new object reference is created
52	whenever a reference object is constructed,
53	so that reference objects constructed separately are always distinct.
54	What about reference objects that have no mutable fields?
55	Reference objects include
56	strings
57	and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets.
58	\revision{revival-object-kinds}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named
59	arbitrary-precision numbers among the reference objects and gave strings no
60	kind.
61	The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that the values of the
62	arbitrary-precision integer and rational types are value objects, as \library\
63	declare them, and on 6 and 7~November 2026 that strings are reference objects:
64	two strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and their
65	text equality is their \EXP{=}.}
66	%
67	Function objects are immutable and have no fields.  Identity is not
68	well-defined for function objects, and attempting to check whether two
69	functions are equivalent returns an approximate result.
70	\secref{equivalence} describes object equivalence in further detail.

4021	decisions of the revival.

4023	and rational types are value objects: \library\ declare the arbitrary-precision
4024	integer as a value object, and the sentence's own list called integers value

4027	deliberate word.

4029	\secref{equivalence} on both implementations, with no special case for any type,
4030	and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
4031	object without the \KWD{value} modifier, so two strings are strictly equivalent
4032	only when they are one object, and their text equality is their own \EXP{=}.
4033	The Working Draft of February 2011 named no kind for strings, and the

2739	\subsection{The conversion into a float, declared by each number type}
2740	\seclabel{revival-asfloat}
2741	
2742	\begin{description}
2743	\item[Affected sections] \secref{basic-rationals}; \secref{revival-numbers}.
2744	\item[Change] The passage on the conversions between number types says that
2745	the explicit conversion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)}, is the
2746	method that each number type declares, and that \TYP{Number} itself declares
2747	no conversion, where it said that \library\ declare the method on
2748	\TYP{Number}.
2749	The change of \secref{revival-numbers} says the same.
2750	\item[Rationale] The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that \VAR{asFloat}, and
2751	the \EXP{=} that the library built on it, leave the trait \TYP{Number}, and that
2752	each of the library's number types keeps its own \VAR{asFloat}.
2753	The team's later compiler library declares \TYP{Number} with nothing in it
2754	(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss}, lines
2755	510--511, in the revival's repository), and declares its conversion into
2756	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} on each of its number types, not on a shared trait; the
2757	Working Draft names no such method.
2758	With \TYP{Number} open to a program's own number types, an abstract
2759	\VAR{asFloat} would oblige a program's complex number to give a float, and an
2760	\EXP{=} on \TYP{Number} built on it would call two different complex numbers
2761	equal.
2762	\Library\ now declare \VAR{asFloat} on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}32},
2763	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
2764	\EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and the numeral type \TYP{IntLiteral}
2765	(\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi};
2766	\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi}), and the vector
2767	norm at each of the eight number types as its element type.
2768	A reversal would declare \VAR{asFloat} on \TYP{Number} again, abstract, with an
2769	\EXP{=} built on it, so that every type below \TYP{Number} must give a float, or
2770	declare it on a new trait that the number types extend.
2771	\item[Effect] \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} is unchanged at every number type of the
2772	library.
2773	Two numbers of different types compare by \EXP{=} where a coercion carries one
2774	into the other: for each of the library's 21 coercions between number types,
2775	the type converted to declares \EXP{=} at the type converted from, and that type
2776	declares \EXP{=} at the first, each converting the narrower operand as the
2777	coercion does.
2778	Two numbers of different types that no coercion joins, as a \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
2779	and an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, compare by the library's fallback \EXP{=} over
2780	\TYP{Any}, which answers \EXP{a \sequiv b}; a program that means their values
2781	writes the conversion, \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x) = y}.
2782	Two values of different types are never strictly equivalent
2783	(\secref{equivalence}), so that fallback answers \VAR{false} for them, on the
2784	interpreter as in the compiled code's helper.
2785	A number type of a program's own compares by the \EXP{=} it declares, or else by
2786	the fallback.
2787	\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 has no such sentence:
2788	the revival added it in its own text of 27~September 2026, not the Working
2789	Draft's.
2790	The passage said, in \nolinkurl{Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex}, lines
2791	46--49, before this revision:
2792	\begin{quote}
2793	Every other conversion between number types is written explicitly;
2794	in particular, a conversion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from
2795	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
2796	is explicit, written \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} with the method that \library\ declare on \TYP{Number}.
2797	\end{quote}
2798	and the change of \secref{revival-numbers} said that the conversion into
2799	\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} is written ``with the method the library declares on
2800	\TYP{Number}''.
2801	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
2802	\end{description}
